result:
`final.py` scores **0.5587** on the search split, against the baseline's 0.365. I used about 19 of the 24 scorer calls over about 10 of the 15 minutes. I'm estimating that count: I couldn't see exactly how many calls the failed runs consumed, which were two syntax-check rejections and one timeout. I did not run a separate held-out score.

**How it works:** `final.py` runs six shadow policies on every request: LRU, ARC, three window-plus-frequency-admission caches (window sizes of 2%, 10% and 30% of capacity) and a LeCaR-style policy that picks between LRU, LFU and most-recently-used eviction. A seventh and eighth variant use faster frequency decay. The real cache follows whichever shadow has the best recent hit rate. It only switches when a rival is clearly ahead. To follow the leader it evicts keys the leader doesn't hold and stores a missed key only if the leader does.

**Search scores of the main candidates:**

| Candidate | Search score |
|---|---|
| LRU baseline | 0.365 |
| ARC | 0.407 |
| LeCaR-style | 0.493 |
| Adaptive-window admission cache | 0.497 |
| Fixed-window admission cache | 0.510 |
| Meta-cache over 6 shadows | 0.551 |
| Meta-cache over 8 shadows, switching tuned | 0.5587 |

**What I found:**
- **Ceiling:** the `hot_with_scans` and `mixed` traces stayed near 0.24 and 0.26 for every policy, so those look close to their limit.
- **Timeout:** one scorer run hit the time limit while the machine was heavily loaded. A cache-eviction bug in the code at the time was also slowing it. After the fix, scorer runs take about 1.3 seconds, but another timeout on a loaded machine is possible.
